newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-United News snaps up HTV for $618 mln.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-United News snaps up HTV for $618 mln.

text.p: Britain's United News & Media Plc on Friday agreed to buy the rest of Welsh and west of England broadcaster HTV Group in a deal valuing HTV at 371.7 million pounds ($618 million).

Amid increasing consolidation in the UK commercial TV sector, United News offered 420 pence per share for HTV in a bid agreed by HTV directors and took control immediately, as it took 51 percent of the company.

United News, which already held almost 30 percent of HTV, is one of Britain's three largest commercial television operators. It also owns Express Newspapers, regional newspapers and business services.

Roger Laughton, the chief executive of United's TV business, United Broadcasting & Entertainment, said the company was keen to develop HTV's broadcasting and rights interests and expected to reap significant synergies.
"There is a compelling strategic case for this acquisition which brings with it clear opportunities for cost savings and revenue growth," he said.

But the move might disappoint rebel insitutional shareholders in Yorkshire-Tyne Tees Television Holdings Plc, who are not supporting a recommended 711 million pound bid from media group Granada Group Plc in the hope of a higher counter offer.

United News had been rumoured to be amongst possible bidders. But Yorkshire's chairman Ward Thomas told Reuters just two days ago United's chief executive Clive Hollick was much more likely to be interested in HTV.

The HTV bid price represents a premium of around 27 percent to the group's closing price on June 26, the last business day before the announcement. The deal will be broadly earnings neutral in its first financial year.
But United said it expected to reap substantial savings from merging the two TV business.

United will keep the regional broadcast and production centres of the two businesses but said the acquisition would enable support functions to be rationalised and savings made in corporate overheads.
HTV employed an average of 643 staff in 1996. It said it had not been told how many employees might lose their jobs as part of the takeover.
HTV's shares, which fell to only 14p each in 1992, shot up 84.5p to close at 415p, just below the offer price. United News saw its stock end 10.5p lower at 713.5p.

The size of the bid surprised some traders, because it is on a higher earnings multiple than previous offers in a sector. However, one analyst said: "There is a consolidation going on in the industry and they are paying the price they have to pay."

The acquisition of HTV will consolidate United News's position as a significant participant in ITV commercial television. The company's share of advertising revenue will jump to 24 percent from 18 percent and its share of the country's audience will rise to eight percent from around five percent, a spokesman said.
Louis Sherwood, the chairman of HTV, said that he firmly believed that the offer was good for shareholders.
"We have also been reassured by United's commitment to maintain an appropriate focus on our regional programming and our other licence obligations," he added. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
